people.name: Mike Elliott
body: On election night in November 2018, voters in Brooklyn Center, an inner-ring suburb north of Minneapolis, chose a man who had left Liberia at 11. Mike Elliott won with 55 percent of the vote and became the city's first Black mayor and the first Liberian American to hold the office.

Some history helps here. Liberia was founded in the 1820s by formerly enslaved Black Americans resettled on the West African coast, so its ties to the United States run deep. Its civil wars, from 1989 to 2003, drove many people from the country, and many families rebuilt their lives in the northern suburbs of the Twin Cities.

NBC News reported that Elliott's grandmother helped him leave Liberia while his mother was already in the U.S. At Brooklyn Center High School, classmates elected him class president. He graduated from Hamline University in St. Paul with a degree in international management. Before running for office he started a translation company and a tutoring nonprofit, Fastforward Education. His first run for mayor, in 2014, fell short.

In April 2021 a Brooklyn Center police officer shot and killed 20-year-old Daunte Wright during a traffic stop. In the days that followed, the City Council gave the mayor command authority over the police department and fired the city manager, and the police chief resigned. The city later passed the Daunte Wright and Kobe Dimock-Heisler Community Safety and Violence Prevention Act.

Elliott lost his bid for a second term in November 2022 to the current mayor, and his last council meeting was that December. "Let's celebrate our differences, and let's also celebrate what we have in common," he said in his parting remarks, according to CCX Media.
keyFacts: Left Liberia at 11, with his grandmother's help, according to NBC News.
Graduated from Brooklyn Center High School and Hamline University.
2014: Lost his first mayoral race.
2018: Elected mayor with 55 percent of the vote; first Black and first Liberian American mayor of Brooklyn Center.
April 2021: Led the city after the police killing of Daunte Wright.
November 2022: Lost his race for a second term.
people.connectToWork: When a crisis puts one official or one organization at the center of public attention, whose voices does your agency stop hearing, and how would you find out?

people.name: Wynfred Russell
people.field: Local government, public health, nonprofit leadership
body: In January 2019 Wynfred Russell took the oath of office as a Brooklyn Park City Council member with his hand on his late father's Bible. Relatives in Brooklyn Park and in Liberia watched live. He became the first Liberian American on the council of a city that FOX 9 called home to the country's largest Liberian population.

FOX 9 reported that he grew up in a refugee camp in Africa, won a college scholarship, and came to Minnesota when the University of Minnesota hired him. He credited his parents with his commitment to public life: his father was active in church and community, and his mother was a longtime schoolteacher.

Before holding office, he founded African Career, Education & Resource, Inc. (ACER), an organization that works with immigrant and underserved communities in the north and northwest suburbs. His own account also lists international public health work, including Ebola response in Liberia and polio eradication in Nigeria, and service on Brooklyn Park's Planning Commission and Human Rights Commission and the Hennepin County Library Board.
His first run for the council seat ended in a loss by five votes. Six years later, in 2018, he defeated incumbent Bob Mata with 55 percent of the vote.

As of October 2026 he describes himself as a former council member, a public health professional and a nonprofit executive. He ran in the August 11, 2026 DFL primary for Minnesota House District 38A, where the incumbent state representative won with 48.8 percent (1,822 votes) to his 41.8 percent (1,561), with Richard Klatte at 9.4 percent. Russell had also lost the 2024 primary by 50 votes.
keyFacts: Grew up in a refugee camp in Africa before a college scholarship, according to FOX 9.
Founded ACER.
Lost a Brooklyn Park council race by five votes, then won the seat in 2018 with 55 percent.
January 2019: Sworn in as Brooklyn Park's first Liberian American council member.
Former council member. Lost the August 11, 2026 DFL primary for Minnesota House District 38A, with 41.8 percent to the incumbent state representative's 48.8 percent.

people.name: Wokie Freeman
people.field: Public administration, university programs, youth organizations
body: Mshale, the Twin Cities newspaper for African immigrants, reported that Wokie Freeman left Liberia with her family in 1990 as a teenager, as civil war spread. The family settled in Brooklyn Park, where she finished high school before studying chemistry at the University of Minnesota. Decades later she returned to the same city's government as assistant city manager.

Her career shows the less visible side of public life. She spent 12 years at the University of Minnesota, most recently as assistant executive director and director of operations and programs at the Robert J. Jones Urban Research and Outreach-Engagement Center. As a volunteer she was founding director of public affairs and engagement for ACER.

At Brooklyn Park she served six years as assistant city manager and director of the administration department. The city credited her with overseeing human resources, the city clerk's office, information technology, community engagement, communications, and racial equity work. It also credited her with the city's police scorecard work and its Sister City policy. The city proclaimed July 22, 2022, her last day, as Wokie Freeman-Gbogba Day.
As of October 2026 Youthprise, a Minneapolis nonprofit focused on young people, lists her as its senior operations officer.
keyFacts: 1990: Left Liberia as a teenager, according to Mshale.
12 years at the University of Minnesota, including its Urban Research and Outreach-Engagement Center.
Six years as Brooklyn Park assistant city manager; last day July 22, 2022.
As of October 2026: Senior operations officer at Youthprise.

people.name: Abdullah Kiatamba
body: In the fall of 2014 the Ebola epidemic was devastating Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea, and a Liberian man who had traveled to Texas had just been diagnosed with the disease. Abdullah Kiatamba, a Liberian immigrant, headed the Minnesota African Task Force Against Ebola.

He told MPR News that "a lot of people are worried in Minnesota." He urged people to postpone travel to the affected countries, and he said he feared that Minnesota's immigrant community could be stigmatized if someone came back sick.

He was executive director of African Immigrant Services in Brooklyn Park. In May 2017, when the federal government ended temporary protected status for West Africans from the Ebola-affected countries, he called the decision premature and "heartbreaking and troubling." He estimated that 200 to 500 people in Minnesota would lose status, because officials were not releasing state figures. MPR News identified him in the same role in 2018, when Liberians faced the end of Deferred Enforced Departure.
keyFacts: 2014: Headed the Minnesota African Task Force Against Ebola.
May 2017: Opposed the end of temporary protected status for West Africans from Ebola-affected countries.
2018: Identified by MPR News as executive director of African Immigrant Services.
people.connectToWork: When a health emergency or a federal decision reaches people you serve, what would you need to have in place beforehand so that your message does not add to fear or stigma?

people.name: Prince Cole
body: Prince Cole grew up in Liberia. He became sick as a teenager and lost the use of his legs and one arm. "If you have disabilities in Liberia, like society don't count you amongst the population," he told WCCO in 2024. "I was rejected, I was neglected." This is one person's experience, not a survey.

He and his wife, Agnes, who was born with one leg shorter than the other, moved to the United States and settled in Blaine, Minnesota. One day a friend with disabilities called Agnes from Liberia to say people were starving and that two children with disabilities had died. In a Minnesota snowstorm, Prince went to the bank and sent every penny they had, $110. That was the start of the Disability Motivational Network.

According to WCCO, the couple went on to build an accessible orphanage and an accessible clinic in Liberia. By 2024 they supported more than 100 residents and 300 schoolchildren, and had put 20 children through to college.
keyFacts: Lives in Blaine, Minnesota.
Co-founded the Disability Motivational Network with his wife, Agnes Cole; its own page dates it to 2016.
2024: WCCO reported more than 100 residents, 300 schoolchildren and 20 young people in college.

people.name: Patricia Jabbeh Wesley
body: In June 2008 Hamline University in St. Paul hosted public hearings of Liberia's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, so that Liberians who had fled the civil wars could tell their stories on the record. Among those called to testify was Patricia Jabbeh Wesley, a poet and scholar named an expert witness. She spoke about her own wartime experiences and her research on Liberian women's war stories.

Wesley was born in Monrovia and earned her bachelor's degree at the University of Liberia. During the civil war she came to the United States with her family, settling in Michigan in 1991. She went on to earn a master's degree at Indiana University Bloomington and a PhD in creative writing and literature from Western Michigan University.

Her poetry carries war, displacement and motherhood across the diaspora. Her books include Before the Palm Could Bloom (1998), Becoming Ebony (2003), which won the Crab Orchard Award, The River Is Rising (2007), Where the Road Turns (2010), When the Wanderers Come Home (2016), and Praise Song for My Children (2020), which won the 2023 Theodore Roethke Memorial Poetry Award. She also received the 2022 Levinson Prize and the 2021 Edward Stanley Award. In 2023 she edited Breaking the Silence: Anthology of Liberian Poetry.

The Academy of American Poets lists her as a professor at Penn State Altoona, where she teaches English, creative writing and African literature. From 2003 to 2008 she chaired the African Literature Division of the Modern Language Association.
keyFacts: Born in Monrovia; bachelor's degree from the University of Liberia.
1991: Moved to Michigan with her family during the civil war.
June 2008: Expert witness at the Truth and Reconciliation Commission hearings in St. Paul.
2023: Theodore Roethke Memorial Poetry Award; edited an anthology of Liberian poetry.

people.name: Emmanuel Matadi
body: At the Rio de Janeiro Olympics in August 2016, a sprinter from St. Paul carried the flag of Liberia into the opening ceremony. Emmanuel Matadi led a delegation of just two athletes. A few years earlier, his running career had seemed to be over.

Matadi was born in Liberia in 1991. His family fled in 1999 and settled briefly in California before moving to St. Paul. He first tried track at Cleveland Junior High and did not like it, and he came back to sprinting after an injury ended his football plans. At Johnson Senior High School he became a state champion sprinter.

College was not a straight line, but he found his stride at Minnesota State University, Mankato. In a single season there he set school records in the 100, 200 and 4x100 relay and won NCAA Division II titles in the 100 and 200 meters in 2015. Life outside the track was hard: on the day he committed to Mankato, a fire destroyed his family's St. Paul home.

He went on to compete for Liberia at the Rio, Tokyo and Paris Olympics. He won bronze in the 200 at the 2016 African Championships. At Paris in 2024, in his third Games, he ran 10.08 seconds in his heat and advanced to the 100-meter semifinals.
keyFacts: Born in Liberia in 1991; family fled in 1999 and settled in St. Paul after a stay in California.
State champion sprinter at Johnson Senior High School.
2015: NCAA Division II champion in the 100 and 200 meters for Minnesota State, Mankato.
2016: Liberia's flag bearer at the Rio Olympics.
2024: Reached the Olympic 100-meter semifinals in Paris.

people.name: Wilmot Collins
people.field: Local government, child protection, military service
body: Late on a September evening in 1990, Wilmot Collins and his wife, Maddie, boarded a cargo ship to flee Liberia's civil war. They went first to Ghana. Maddie had once spent a year in Montana as a high school exchange student, and in 1991 she arrived in Helena on a nursing scholarship to Carroll College. Collins's refugee screening took 31 months before he could join her there in February 1994.

He worked at a home for abused children and as a school janitor, then as a state child protection specialist, a teacher and a Veterans Affairs administrator, and he served 22 years in the U.S. Navy Reserve. His wife became a VA nurse and served in the Army Reserve, and their daughter joined the Navy.

In November 2017 Collins ran for mayor of Montana's capital on promises of affordable housing, attention to homelessness among veterans and teenagers, and more police and firefighters. He defeated four-term mayor Jim Smith, 51 percent to 48 percent. The Carnegie Corporation calls him the first Black mayor of any Montana city since statehood. The Montana Historical Society notes that Edward W. Johnson, a barber from Washington, D.C., became the first mayor of unincorporated Helena in 1874.

As mayor he hosted monthly "Wednesdays with Wilmot" sessions, and in 2019 he announced a run for the U.S. Senate. As of October 2026 he is no longer mayor; Helena's mayor is Emily Dean, who gave the State of the City address in January 2026. He has published a book, Run: The Wilmot Collins Story.
keyFacts: September 1990: Fled Liberia by cargo ship with his wife.
February 1994: Joined her in Helena after a 31-month refugee process.
22 years in the U.S. Navy Reserve; worked in child protection and veterans' services.
November 2017: Elected mayor of Helena, 51 percent to 48 percent.
2019: Named a Great Immigrant by the Carnegie Corporation of New York.

people.name: Naquetta Ricks
body: Naquetta Ricks was born in Liberia. In 1980, after a military coup in which her mother's fiancé, a government official, was killed, she fled with her mother and sister. They settled in Aurora, Colorado, where she graduated from Aurora Central High School.

She earned a bachelor's degree in accounting from Metropolitan State University of Denver and an MBA from the University of Colorado Denver, and she runs a mortgage brokerage. She also co-founded and leads the African Chamber of Commerce of Colorado.

She ran for the Aurora City Council in 2017. In 2020 she won a seat in the Colorado House of Representatives from District 40, and she was sworn in on January 13, 2021. The Sentinel described her as the first African immigrant elected to Colorado's legislature, and her caucus describes her as the first Liberian American elected to a state legislature. Rhode Island's Nathan Biah was elected the same month.
As of October 2026 the Colorado General Assembly lists her as the representative for District 40 and chair of the House Business Affairs and Labor Committee.

people.name: Nathan Biah
body: Nathan Biah was born in Monrovia on December 4, 1971. At 20 he escaped the civil war by walking nearly 90 miles, and he came to the United States as a refugee.

He settled in Providence, Rhode Island, where he earned his GED while working in a factory. He earned a criminal justice degree from Rhode Island College in 1999 and a master's in education administration from the University of Rhode Island in 2007. He taught math in Providence middle and high schools and became principal of Dr. Jorge Alvarez High School.

In September 2020 he challenged incumbent Moira Walsh in the Democratic primary for Rhode Island's House District 3 and won 491 votes to 267. He was elected that November, the same month as Colorado's Naquetta Ricks. In 2023 he entered the race for Rhode Island's 1st Congressional District, then ended that campaign in June to seek an open state Senate seat.

As of October 2026 the Rhode Island General Assembly lists him as the representative for District 3, serving on the House Finance, Education, and Innovation and Technology committees, and as principal of Alvarez High School. His 2026 bills include one that would require nursing assistant licensing exams in English and Spanish.

people.name: Helene Cooper
body: Helene Cooper spent her early childhood in a large house on a beach about eleven miles outside Monrovia, in a family among Liberia's settler-descended elite, known as the "Honorables." In 1980 a military coup led by Master Sergeant Samuel Doe overthrew the government, and the violence that followed reached her family directly. At 13 she fled with her family to the United States.

That story became her memoir, The House at Sugar Beach (2008), a finalist for the National Book Critics Circle Award. In it, Cooper looks honestly at the divide in Liberian society between the descendants of Black American settlers and the poorer "Country" people of the Indigenous majority. That divide is useful background for the 1980 coup and the wars that followed.

She spent twelve years at The Wall Street Journal as a reporter and foreign correspondent, then joined The New York Times, where her roles have included assistant editorial page editor, White House correspondent, diplomatic correspondent and Pentagon correspondent. She was part of the Times team that won the 2015 Pulitzer Prize for International Reporting for its coverage of the Ebola epidemic. She also wrote Madame President (2017), a biography of Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, Liberia's first elected woman president.

Fled to the U.S. at 13 after the 1980 military coup.
2008: Published The House at Sugar Beach.

2015: Part of the New York Times team that won a Pulitzer Prize for Ebola coverage.

people.name: Wayétu Moore
body: When Wayétu Moore was five, in 1990, war forced her family out of Monrovia. She walked for three weeks with her father and sisters to a village near the Sierra Leone border, where they stayed for months. Her mother, Mamawa Freeman-Moore, was studying at Teachers College, Columbia University, on a Fulbright, and had no news of them, so she flew to Sierra Leone. A teenage rebel fighter risked her life to bring the family across the border to her. They later settled in Texas.

Moore told that story in her memoir, The Dragons, the Giant, the Women (2020), which sets a child's sense of wonder against the facts of war and then follows her through growing up Black and immigrant in America. It was a New York Times Notable Book and a National Book Critics Circle Award finalist, and in 2022 it won the nonfiction award of the William Saroyan International Prize for Writing.

Her debut novel, She Would Be King (2018), retells Liberia's founding through magical realism. Moore received a 2019 Lannan Literary Fellowship. A graduate of Howard University, the University of Southern California and Columbia University, she also founded One Moore Book, a publisher of children's books for readers in countries underrepresented in literature, beginning with Liberia.

Founded One Moore Book, a children's publisher.
2018: Published She Would Be King.

2022: William Saroyan International Prize for nonfiction.

people.name: Tamba Hali
body: Civil war broke out in Liberia when Tamba Hali was six. His family made a risky escape into Côte d'Ivoire and eventually reached a monastery in Ghana. His father, Henry, a science teacher who had reached America years earlier, worked through a complicated process to bring the children to the United States. Tamba left Africa in 1992, as a child. His mother, Rachel Keita, had to stay behind.

In New Jersey he attended Teaneck High School and went on to Penn State, where he became a consensus All-American. The Kansas City Chiefs drafted him in the first round in 2006, and he spent his entire 12-season career with the team. He made five straight Pro Bowls from 2011 to 2015. His 89.5 career sacks rank second in franchise history, and he was a 2014 nominee for the Walter Payton NFL Man of the Year award, which recognizes community service.

In 2016 he returned to Liberia for the first time since 1992, reconnecting with relatives he had not seen in about two decades and meeting President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf. In 2024 the Chiefs inducted him into their Hall of Honor.

people.name: Telfar Clemens
body: At the Tokyo Olympics opening ceremony in July 2021, Liberia's small team walked out in clothes unlike any other nation's: unisex unitards, one-shouldered tank tops, loose tracksuits, and a traditional lappa wrap reimagined in navy jersey, with large stars echoing Liberia's flag. The designer was Telfar Clemens, a Liberian American from Queens.

Clemens was born in 1985 in Lefrak City, Queens, to Liberian parents. The family moved back to Liberia for a short time, then returned to Queens in 1990. A monogram a grade school teacher drew for him became the logo of his unisex label, Telfar, which he founded in 2005 while studying business management at Pace University.

His best-known product, the Telfar Shopping Bag, is a faux-leather tote nicknamed the "Bushwick Birkin." In 2017 he won the CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund, whose $400,000 prize let him produce the bag at scale, and in 2020 the CFDA named him American Accessories Designer of the Year.

With business partner Babak Radboy, he became the Liberian team's official sponsor in June 2021. The Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology later purchased one of the 2021 jerseys and showed it in its exhibition Africa's Fashion Diaspora.

2021: Designed Liberia's Tokyo Olympics uniforms and sponsored the team.

people.name: Darlington Nagbe
body: In September 2015 Darlington Nagbe became a U.S. citizen. About two months later he pulled on a United States national team jersey for the first time.

Nagbe was born in Monrovia on July 19, 1990. His father, Joe Nagbe, was a professional player and a former captain of Liberia's national team. When Darlington was about five months old his mother fled the civil war with him and his siblings. The family followed his father's career through several countries, including France, Greece and Switzerland, before settling in Cleveland when he was 11. He later played for Lakewood High School in Ohio.

At the University of Akron he led the Zips to the 2010 College Cup, the school's first national team title in any sport, and won the Hermann Trophy. The Portland Timbers drafted him second overall in 2011. He won MLS Cup with Portland in 2015, Atlanta United in 2018, and the Columbus Crew in 2020 and 2023, became Columbus's captain, and was named the club's most valuable player in 2025.

He earned 25 caps for the United States and played in the 2017 Gold Cup final. He retired as a player after the 2025 season, and USSoccerPlayers.com reports that he joined the Columbus coaching staff.
keyFacts: Born July 19, 1990, in Monrovia; son of former Liberia captain Joe Nagbe.
Left Liberia at about five months; settled in Cleveland at 11.
2010: College Cup champion and Hermann Trophy winner at Akron.
September 2015: Became a U.S. citizen; 25 caps for the U.S.
MLS Cup champion in 2015, 2018, 2020 and 2023; retired after 2025.

people.name: Saycon Sengbloh
body: In early 2016 Eclipsed, Danai Gurira's play about Liberian women held captive by a rebel officer during the Second Liberian Civil War, moved from a sold-out run at The Public Theater to Broadway. One of the leads was Saycon Sengbloh, the daughter of a Liberian father and an American mother. Her performance earned a 2016 Tony nomination, the 2016 Drama Desk Award for Outstanding Featured Actress in a Play, and an Obie Award.

Sengbloh, an Atlanta native who began acting at the Tri-Cities School for the Visual and Performing Arts and later attended Agnes Scott College, built a long Broadway career in musicals, including Aida, Wicked, The Color Purple, Hair, Fela! and Motown: The Musical. Eclipsed was her first straight play. On television she played Lillian Williams in The Wonder Years.

Eclipsed had personal meaning for her. Her father, who was born in Liberia and died in 1999, had supported her career, and she told NBC News she wished he could see her "doing this Liberian role." Preparing for the part also led her to talk with her older sister about the war, a subject they had rarely discussed.
keyFacts: Atlanta native with a Liberian father and an American mother.
2015–2016: Starred in Eclipsed at The Public Theater and on Broadway.
2016: Drama Desk Award and Obie Award; Tony nomination.
Played Lillian Williams in The Wonder Years.

people.name: Naomi B. Harris
body: Naomi B. Harris led Liberia's National Union of Organizations of the Disabled (NUOD), which the African Disability Rights Yearbook describes as the country's largest coalition of disabled people's organizations. She was paralyzed in one leg at age 2 and walked with crutches.

She first won the presidency in 2017. On March 29, 2019, she was re-elected at a congress in Monrovia. "My victory in the election today is a proof of my people's confidence in me," she told reporters, according to FrontPage Africa.

As president she spoke for disabled Liberians before lawmakers and in the counties, pressed the government to employ disabled people, and told audiences that "disability is not for one person." She died on February 26, 2022. FrontPage Africa called her NUOD's longest-serving president. She lived and worked in Liberia, and her name appears here because Liberian disability rights leadership is part of the history behind this page.
keyFacts: 2017: First elected president of NUOD.
March 29, 2019: Re-elected.
February 26, 2022: Died; succeeded in 2023 by Peter B. K. Flomo.

institutions.name: Organization of Liberians in Minnesota
body: "This community has always craved for a community center," executive director Kamaty Diahn told CCX Media in July 2026, after the Minnesota Legislature included $400,000 for the Organization of Liberians in Minnesota in that year's bonding bill. The money will expand and remodel OLM's Brooklyn Park facility, with more room for youth and senior programs.
The grant capped years of effort. In 2021 the group was raising money for a down payment to expand its space. Bills in the 2024 and 2025 sessions proposed the same one-time grant.

OLM says its mission is to provide social services to immigrants and refugees in education, housing, health and employment. It runs community, senior and youth enrichment programs, and it advocates for Liberians on Temporary Protected Status and Deferred Enforced Departure. In 2021 the Brooklyn Park Economic Development Authority funded an OLM program to train 60 city residents, of any background, as nursing assistants and medication aides. The Sun Post reported in 2022 that 42 students went on to jobs.

OLM's site names the Liberia Ministers Association, Masjid Al-Ansar Islamic Community Center, African Immigrant Services, and Liberian county and tribal associations among its partners. Its members elect a nine-member board every two years.
keyFacts: Founded in 1973 and incorporated in 1979, by its own account.
Executive director as of 2026: Kamaty Diahn.
2021: Partnered with Brooklyn Park on health care job training.
2026: $400,000 in the state bonding bill to expand and remodel its center.
institutions.connectToWork: If you asked this kind of organization to help you reach people, what would you offer in return, and how would you avoid treating one organization as the whole community?

institutions.name: We Are Liberian
body: On July 26, 2025, Liberia's Independence Day, a parade stepped off on Shingle Creek Parkway in Brooklyn Center and ended at Centennial Park. By CCX Media's account it was the first Liberian Independence Day parade in Minnesota, marking 35 years of Liberians in the United States, with about 70 vendors and Liberian music, food and artifacts. Sahan Journal reported that thousands came, some from as far as New York. The organizer was We Are Liberian, a local nonprofit co-founded by Marie Dweh, who also runs a home health care business.

"This was something that started off as two people," Dweh told Sahan Journal. In 2026 the parade and festival moved to North Hennepin Community College in Brooklyn Park, again on July 26, a Sunday; Sahan Journal's text mentions a Saturday morning parade, while its listing gives Sunday, July 26. A planned Minnesota United match against Liberia at Allianz Field on July 26, 2026, which OLM advertised, was canceled over visa denials.
Dweh describes the purpose plainly: "Our whole mission is to bridge the gap between the older generation and the new generation."
keyFacts: Co-founded by Marie Dweh.
July 26, 2025: First Liberian Independence Day parade in Minnesota, in Brooklyn Center.
July 26, 2026: Parade and free festival at North Hennepin Community College.

institutions.name: Liberia TRC Diaspora Project
aliases: The Advocates for Human Rights Liberia project
institutions.location: Minneapolis–St. Paul, with sites across the diaspora
body: In June 2008 Liberia's Truth and Reconciliation Commission held public hearings at Hamline University in St. Paul. The Advocates for Human Rights, based in Minneapolis, calls them the first public hearings of a national truth commission held in a diaspora. More than 20 witnesses testified.

More than 600 volunteers helped the project document statements from more than 1,600 Liberians in the diaspora, at sites including Minneapolis–St. Paul, Atlanta, Chicago, Philadelphia, Washington, D.C., New York City, Providence, Boston, the United Kingdom, and the Buduburam refugee settlement in Ghana.

Liberia created its commission by an act passed in 2005, after the wars ended in 2003. It looked at violations from January 1979 to October 2003 and completed its work on June 30, 2009. The diaspora project's final report, A House with Two Rooms, was published in 2009.
The project made Minnesota a site of Liberian national history, not only a place of refuge. Poet Patricia Jabbeh Wesley was named an expert witness.
keyFacts: 2005: Liberia's Truth and Reconciliation Commission established by act.
June 2008: Hearings at Hamline University, St. Paul.
More than 1,600 diaspora statements; more than 600 volunteers.
2009: Final report, A House with Two Rooms.

institutions.name: Disability Motivational Network
institutions.location: Blaine, Minnesota, with programs in Liberia
body: Prince and Agnes Cole of Blaine started the network with their own savings. Its GiveMN page says it works to meet basic health care and education needs for children and adults with disabilities in Liberia, and to change attitudes so that they are valued in their communities.

WCCO reported in 2024 that it had built an accessible orphanage for abandoned children and an accessible clinic, and that the couple was seeking donations of medical equipment and furniture. Its own site lists shelter, meals, medicine, free education and scholarships, mobility aids, and a disability support group that meets on the last Saturday of each month.
It is Minnesota-rooted, but its programs are in Liberia. It is not a Minnesota service provider.
keyFacts: Founded in 2016; a 501(c)(3) based in Blaine.
2024: More than 100 residents, 300 schoolchildren and 20 young people in college, according to WCCO.

institutions.name: National Union of Organizations of the Disabled, Liberia
institutions.dates: Created in 1995, by its president's account
body: The African Disability Rights Yearbook's 2020 report describes NUOD as Liberia's largest coalition of disabled people's organizations, with about 17 member bodies. It belongs to the Alliance on Disability, a group of six organizations that advocates for carrying out the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which Liberia ratified in 2012. The report names funding as the biggest challenge for these groups.

NUOD's leadership changed in 2023, when Peter B. K. Flomo was elected president. In a report that year, FrontPage Africa described a four-year plan that includes the legislative representation promised in Liberia's 2005 disability law and a permanent headquarters. "Since the creation of NUOD in 1995, we have squatted in more than seven places," Flomo said.
keyFacts: About 17 member bodies, as of the 2020 report.
Member of the Alliance on Disability.
2023: Peter B. K. Flomo elected president.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Liberian means people with personal or family roots in Liberia, who differ by generation, by when and how they or their families left, and by faith, county, ethnic group and education. We did not find published research on how Liberian Americans in Minnesota, or anywhere in the U.S., understand disability. Almost everything below comes from Liberia itself: a legal report, a medical group's report, news reporting and first-person accounts. One study from neighboring Sierra Leone is labeled as such.
questions: What language or way of speaking is most comfortable for you? Would you like an interpreter, or written materials in plain English?
Who in your family, or outside it, helps you make decisions like this? Would you like them here?
What have you been told about this condition, here or back home? What do you think about it?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it to you, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Are you already getting help from a church, mosque, healer or community group? How can our services work alongside that?
Do you have any worries about how using services might affect your immigration case or your family?
Are you also caring for or supporting anyone in Liberia?
Do you prefer phone or in-person contact, and would written follow-up in plain language help?
If you would like to tell me, what do you understand to have caused this? You do not have to answer.

context.heading: What reports from Liberia describe about explanations and first steps
body: Doctors Without Borders (MSF) reported in February 2020 on its epilepsy care in Montserrado County, where it treated more than 1,300 patients. It said that many patients face neglect and stigma because some people wrongly believe epilepsy is contagious, that relatives sometimes abandon patients out of fear, and that some people attribute seizures to causes such as demon possession and turn to traditional healers. This is one program's account of its patients in one county.

A New Narratives report published by FrontPage Africa on August 5, 2026, describes mothers of children with complex needs in Liberia. One mother's community called her daughter, who has cerebral palsy, a dragon, and some pastors claimed a snake had been sent on the child. She believed them at first and later learned the condition was medical.

These accounts do not describe anyone in Minnesota. Ask what the person has been told and what they think. If someone uses prayer, a pastor or imam, or remedies, ask how services can sit alongside that, and do not ask them to choose.

sources.label: Doctors Without Borders, Liberia: A growing cohort of epilepsy patients (February 3, 2020)
FrontPage Africa / New Narratives, They Called Her a Dragon (August 5, 2026)

context.heading: A related study from Sierra Leone
body: This study is from a neighboring country, not Liberia. Carew and colleagues interviewed 32 women with disabilities and 10 women without disabilities in Sierra Leone, published in 2023. Participants said that community beliefs linking disability to witchcraft discouraged women with disabilities from seeking sexual and reproductive health services. Participants also rejected many negative assumptions about their lives.

sources.label: Carew and colleagues, Culture, Health & Sexuality 26(3), 2023

context.heading: Rights, leadership and mutual support
body: Stigma is not the whole picture. The African Disability Rights Yearbook's 2020 report records Liberia's 2005 National Commission on Disabilities Act, its 2012 ratification of the UN disability convention, a coalition of about 17 disabled people's organizations, and the phrase "disability is not inability." It also documents discrimination against children and women with disabilities, verbal and physical attacks on people with albinism, and widespread discrimination in employment.

In the New Narratives report, the King's Kids support group grew from conversations between an American missionary whose daughter has cerebral palsy and a Liberian grandmother raising a grandson with disabilities. It offers practical training and fellowship, and its name tells families their children are not witches, dragons or cursed. In Minnesota, Prince and Agnes Cole, both disabled, built the Disability Motivational Network from $110 of savings.
Do not assume stigma is present. Ask about it only as the person's own experience.

CBS Minnesota (WCCO), Prince and Agnes Cole (July 16, 2024)

context.heading: How much is known about numbers
body: The 2020 Yearbook report says Liberia's 2008 census counted 110,260 people with disabilities (53,698 female and 56,562 male), and that these statistics are outdated and likely an undercount. The figure of 16 percent often quoted in Liberia comes from a 1997 UNICEF study, not the census. Neither figure describes Liberians in Minnesota. We found no count of disabled Liberian Minnesotans.

sources.label: African Disability Rights Yearbook, Country report: Liberia (2020)

context.heading: Immigration status and using services
body: Many Liberians in Minnesota lived for years under temporary legal protections. MPR News reported in 2018 that Deferred Enforced Departure dated back nearly 30 years, and in 2017 that temporary protected status for West Africans from Ebola-affected countries was ending. Sahan Journal reported that a law signed December 20, 2019, opened green card applications to Liberian nationals living continuously in the U.S. since November 20, 2014, along with spouses and children under 21. Deferred Enforced Departure for Liberians was extended only through June 30, 2026, and the Immigration Policy Tracking Project reports it was allowed to expire on that date; the 2019 law was the route to green cards for most long-term residents.

A worry that using services could affect someone's status is a plausible barrier, but we did not find a source that documents it for disability services among Liberian Minnesotans. Give accurate information or refer to an immigration legal service, rather than guessing.

MPR News, Welcome ends in Minn. for hundreds of West Africans from Ebola regions (May 15, 2017)
Sahan Journal, Minnesota's Liberians find elation, relief in new residency law (January 2020)

context.heading: Stigma in a health emergency
body: This is not about disability, but it is recent local history. In October 2014, during the Ebola epidemic, the head of the Minnesota African Task Force Against Ebola told MPR News that he feared Minnesota's immigrant community could be stigmatized if someone returned sick. Keep that history in mind when planning public health or disability outreach, and check that your message cannot be read as blaming a group.

sources.label: MPR News, Leaders of Minnesota's West African community urge against travel to Liberia (October 5, 2014)

context.heading: Family, caregiving and decisions
body: We found no research specific to how Liberian Americans make decisions about disability. Ask each person who takes part, which may include extended family, elders, faith leaders or relatives in Liberia, and hear the person directly even if family speaks first.

The New Narratives report describes mothers in Liberia carrying most of the care for children with complex needs. That is one report about Liberia, and it does not tell you who provides care in any family here.

sources.label: FrontPage Africa / New Narratives, They Called Her a Dragon (August 5, 2026)

context.heading: Words and language
body: We found no research on words for disability in Liberian languages, or on which words carry stigma, so none are offered here. Liberia's disability law and movement use "persons with disabilities," while older organization names still say "the disabled." Follow each person's own preference.

English is Liberia's official language, and people may also speak Liberian English and languages such as Kpelle, Bassa, Grebo or Vai. Speaking English does not settle whether someone wants language help. Ask, use plain language, check understanding, and offer an interpreter when the person wants one.

sources.label: African Disability Rights Yearbook, Country report: Liberia (2020)

communityRoutes.name: Organization of Liberians in Minnesota
communityRoutes.purpose: Runs community, senior and youth enrichment programs in Brooklyn Park, and offers social services in education, housing, health and employment. It is not a disability provider. We did not find a culturally specific disability organization serving Liberians in Minnesota.

communityRoutes.name: Disability Motivational Network
communityRoutes.purpose: A disability nonprofit based in Blaine and founded by a Liberian couple. Its programs are in Liberia, and its site lists a disability support group that meets on the last Saturday of each month. Ask about the group before referring anyone.

organizations.intro: Minnesota's Liberian organizations and congregations are centered in the northwest suburbs, especially Brooklyn Park and Brooklyn Center. Counts differ, and none is a census: in 2026 Sahan Journal cited Minnesota Compass for more than 20,000 Liberians in the state, CCX Media estimated 35,000, and in 2020 Sahan Journal reported about 30,000 statewide and about 7,000 in Brooklyn Park. We could not find a Liberian-specific radio or television program based in Minnesota. These are starting points for learning. The list is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: African Career, Education & Resource
entries.purpose: Founded by Wynfred Russell. Works on voter and civic engagement, economic development, health equity, housing justice and a Change Leaders Fellowship, and offers health care training scholarships. Its associate director, Denise Butler, is the daughter of Liberian immigrants. Events were posted for October 2026.

entries.name: Ebenezer Community Church
entries.purpose: Founded by Pastors Francis and Christine Tabla, who by the church's own account started with just 8 members, and first called Liberian Community Church. FrontPage Africa reports a $2.8 million building, dedicated after a June 7, 2015, groundbreaking. The Star Tribune called it the largest of the Twin Cities' Liberian churches in 2019. The church's own site now says it has over 800 members; an earlier count, reported by Luther Seminary in 2015, was 432. Ministries include senior adults, youth and young adults.

entries.name: Organization of Liberian Women in Minnesota
entries.type: Mutual aid, health and social services
entries.purpose: Founded in 2013. Its GiveMN page says it assists women and children in need in Minnesota and Liberia, with a focus on community engagement, health and wellness, and domestic violence and abuse. A small organization, with federal filings through fiscal 2025 showing gross receipts under $50,000.

entries.name: Liberian Sporting Association of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Founded by Cletus Constance. Has hosted Independence Day events since 2021, including basketball, girls' kickball and boys' soccer, with attendance growing from about 1,000 in 2021 to about 3,000 the next year, by Sahan Journal's report. Partners with OLM on an annual soccer match; the 2026 match was on July 25. Sahan Journal lists Robbinsdale Armstrong High School at 5 p.m., while OLM's event page lists Northwoods Park Field, 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.
entries.linkLabel: Sahan Journal report on the 2026 celebration

entries.name: Mshale
entries.purpose: Minnesota's longest-running newspaper for African immigrants, founded by Tom Gitaa about 1997, according to MPR News. Publishes at mshale.com and has covered Liberian Independence Day and the Organization of Liberians in Minnesota.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: Covers immigrants and communities of color in Minnesota. Its Liberian coverage includes the 2019 residency law and the 2026 Independence Day festival.

entries.name: CCX Media
entries.location: Brooklyn Park and the northwest Hennepin suburbs
entries.purpose: Local news for the northwest suburbs, with repeated coverage of the Organization of Liberians in Minnesota, health care job training and Independence Day events.

entries.name: KMOJ 89.9 FM
entries.purpose: Began in 1976 and describes itself as the people's station, focused on Minnesota's African American community. Its site is kmojfm.com. We could not find a Liberian-specific program.

entries.name: Union of Liberian Associations in the Americas
entries.purpose: An umbrella for Liberian community associations. FrontPage Africa reviewed its 2025 work in January 2026, including advocacy and humanitarian projects.

entries.name: Liberian Studies Association
entries.location: Conferences rotate; the 2026 conference was at UMass Amherst
entries.purpose: A nonprofit scholarly organization founded in 1968 that studies Liberia and the African continent. Held its 57th annual conference April 23 to 25, 2026.

entries.name: African Communities Together
entries.location: New York and the Washington, D.C. area
entries.purpose: Says it is the nation's largest member-led organization of African immigrants. Works on economic justice, housing, immigration advocacy, civic engagement and language access. It was a plaintiff in African Communities Together v. Trump, the 2019 lawsuit over Deferred Enforced Departure for Liberians.

entries.name: UndocuBlack Network
entries.purpose: A multi-generational network of Black immigrants, founded in January 2016, offering community, resources including mental wellness materials, and advocacy. It was a plaintiff in the 2019 lawsuit over Deferred Enforced Departure for Liberians.

entries.name: Embassy of Liberia in Washington, D.C.
entries.purpose: Handles passports, visas and other consular services for Liberia, and publishes diaspora news.

entries.name: FrontPage Africa
entries.purpose: Covers Liberian politics, health, disability and the diaspora, including Liberians in Minnesota.

entries.name: AllAfrica, Liberia section
entries.purpose: Republishes Liberian papers and other African news in English and French.

entries.name: Radio ELWA 94.5 FM
entries.purpose: A Monrovia Christian station. Reports from the SWLing Post say it began streaming online in March 2026, which makes it reachable from Minnesota.

entries.name: Liberia Broadcasting System
entries.type: International: public radio, TV and online news
entries.purpose: Liberia's public broadcaster, with ELBC radio on 99.9 FM and LNTV. Its news site was posting stories dated October 30, 2026.

entries.name: OK FM 99.5
entries.purpose: A private Monrovia station with news and current affairs. Its site showed stories dated May 2026.

entries.name: Liberian Observer
entries.purpose: A daily founded in 1981 by Kenneth Y. Best and Mae Gene Traub Best, covering politics, business, sports and obituaries. Stanford Libraries lists it among Liberian news sources.
